title: Persona
subtitle: the whole series in release order, spin-offs marked
blurb: Six mainline RPGs, about 366 hours of story — the modern trilogy alone averages 84 hours each, and that is not a typo. The editions, the remakes and the spin-offs add 560 more.
paceLabel: the editions, the remakes and the spin-offs
notes: Revelations, the Persona 2 duology, and 3, 4 and 5 — the entries Wikipedia's own release timeline sets in bold. They are the only rows here that are not optional, because someone who has played those six has played Persona in the sense that matters. Everything else is marked optional and stays out of the finish date unless you tick the box that widens it, so a page that grew to twenty-one rows did not quietly rewrite what finishing this list means.
Editions are notes where the data says fold, rows where it says split.

FES, Portable, Golden and Royal are not sequels — they are the same game with more in it, and the question each time is whether it is really a second sitting. The test is the one the Halo and Gears lists fold their remasters on: does HowLongToBeat time it within 3 hours of the original? FES does, because the site files The Answer, the epilogue FES added, as a separate game — so FES ticks the Persona 3 row and is named in its note. The other three miss, Portable by 18 hours, Golden by 6 and Royal by 4 the other way, so each is its own optional row. None of them asks you to play both: the notes say which to pick.

The two fighting games, the two Persona Q crawlers, the three rhythm games, Strikers, Tactica and the mobile Phantom X are real games, and several are canon — Atlus counts Persona Q inside it. They are optional to a one, and every one of them assumes you have played the game it spins off. Persona Q is a 60-hour dungeon crawler and Q2 another 48, which is exactly why they are not folded into the mainline total.

Wikipedia's release timeline is the roster, and everything on it that has shipped is on this page. The Japan-only mobile and browser games it describes in prose but leaves off the timeline are not: Persona 3: The Night Before, Persona Ain Soph, Persona Mobile Online, the Persona 3 phone side-stories and Persona 4 The Card Battle all closed years ago, and there is nothing left to play. Persona 4 Revival, due 18 February 2027, has a row at zero hours: HowLongToBeat has a record for it and no figure yet, and this list refuses to guess one. Persona 6 is announced without a date, and goes on the day it has one.

HowLongToBeat main-story figures — no side content, no maxed social links, no New Game Plus. They are what people report, not what a box claims, which is why Royal comes in over the game it expands and Golden and Portable come in under theirs. Every released row carries a real one, and Persona 4 Revival carries zero until it is out; nothing here was estimated, and a row whose figure fails the name-and-year check fails this build instead of shipping unweighted.

Game list, release order, years and the mainline split from Wikipedia's Persona (franchise) article and each game's own article; hours from HowLongToBeat main-story figures, verified by name and exact release year.

sections.title: The PS1 years
sections.intro: Before the social links — the original and the two-part sequel, darker and stranger than what followed.

items.note: The PS1 original. The 2009 PSP remake is the usual way to play it now — either edition ticks this row.
First half of the duology — Japan-only until the 2011 PSP release
The direct conclusion — the duology is one story in two games

sections.title: The calendar reinvention
sections.intro: A school year, a dungeon, and a deadline — the structure the series is famous for arrives.

items.note: The calendar reinvention. FES (2007) is its director's cut and ticks this row — HowLongToBeat times the two within 2 hours of each other, because it files The Answer, the epilogue FES added, as a separate 28-hour game. Portable and Reload have rows of their own.

A year in Inaba, a rural town, where a group of students investigate a run of killings tied to a realm behind the television called the Midnight Channel. Golden, the expanded version and the usual pick, has its own row below.

sections.title: Phantom Thieves and after
sections.sub: 2016–2027 · 3 games · 162 hours story · 1 not out yet
sections.intro: The biggest one, the remake that brought Persona 3 up to its standard, and the one doing the same for Persona 4.

items.note: The biggest one — Tokyo, and a group of students who put on thieves' disguises to steal the city's corruption out from under it. Royal, the expanded version, has its own row below.
The ground-up remake of Persona 3 — same story, modern build. Play this or the original, not both.

Not out yet — due 18 February 2027 (20 May 2027 on Switch 2), and the bar stays empty until HowLongToBeat has hours for it. The remake of Persona 4 Golden — the same story, rebuilt to the standard of Royal and Reload.

sections.title: The expanded editions
sections.intro: Not sequels — the same games with more in them. FES folds into Persona 3 because HowLongToBeat times the two within hours of each other; these three miss that mark by too far to call them the same sitting, so they are rows.

items.note: The PSP version of FES's main story: a female protagonist to play as instead, the whole party under your control in battle, and content adjusted or cut to fit a handheld. HowLongToBeat times it 18 hours under the PS2 original, which is a different sitting, not a different edition.
The Vita version, and the one most people mean by Persona 4: two new social links, a new character in Marie, extra Personas and more voiced scenes. Play this or the PS2 original, not both.

The rework: a new Palace, a new party member, a new district of Tokyo and a playable third semester on top of everything the 2016 game had. The longest thing on this list. Play this or the original, not both.

sections.title: The spin-offs
sections.intro: Fighting games, dungeon crawlers, rhythm games, a Warriors game, a tactics game and a phone game. All optional, and every one of them assumes you have finished the game it spins off.

items.note: A fighting game co-developed with Arc System Works, and a real sequel: a visual-novel story mode set two months after the Inaba murders close
The follow-up: Japanese arcades in 2013, consoles worldwide in 2014, which is the release HowLongToBeat times. Eight more fighters, and a story mode split into one campaign per game's cast.

items.t: Persona Q: Shadow of the Labyrinth
items.note: A 3DS dungeon crawler dropping the Persona 3 and 4 casts into one labyrinth. Atlus counts it inside the canon, and at 60 hours it runs longer than any of the PS1 games.
The rhythm game, set after Arena Ultimax, and the one of the three built around a full story mode — the 2018 pair dropped it for character interactions instead
One half of a pair released together on purpose — the Persona 3 soundtrack, original and remixed, with S.E.E.S. dancing to it
The other half, released the same day, Phantom Thieves instead of S.E.E.S.
The crawler sequel, adding the Persona 5 cast to the crossover. Japan in 2018, worldwide the year after.
A Dynasty Warriors-style action sequel: four months after Persona 5, the Phantom Thieves reunite for a summer camping trip. The closest thing the series has to a numbered follow-up.
Turn-based tactics with the Phantom Thieves — a different genre wearing the same cast

A free-to-play mobile spin-off with its own cast and its own Tokyo, built by Black Wings Game Studio rather than Atlus. Personas are pulled from a gacha, so the figure beside it is what HowLongToBeat times today rather than a fixed length.
